articles.title_orig: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
articles.title_zh: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has announced new restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips amid fallout from the alleged spy scandal involving AI giant Nvidia.
The rule announced by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) on Monday aims to prevent Chinese AI developers from getting around export controls by remotely accessing data centres in third countries, particularly in Southeast Asia.
It designates Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as countries with an “unacceptable risk of diversion” and requires anyone seeking to ship advanced chips to those destinations to obtain an export licence.
BIS, which sits under the Department of Commerce, said the change was a “logical extension” of the existing requirement for companies to obtain a licence to export or transfer chips to firms based in China.
“The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” BIS said in a statement.
While Chinese firms are barred from importing the most advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) under US export controls, they had until now been legally able to take advantage of remote access to top-of-the-line computing power at data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
Singapore, which hosts dozens of data centres, said on Tuesday that it was “studying the details of this new measure carefully”.
“We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses,” the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information said in a joint statement.
“We have also been engaging the relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies.”
The ministries added that they did not condone companies using Singapore to “circumvent or violate” the laws of other countries.
The restrictions come as Nvidia’s export of advanced chips is under scrutiny following claims that former CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a woman recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security for espionage.
Huang, who became one of the most prominent faces of the AI boom at the helm of Nvidia, resigned last week amid a company board investigation into allegations involving the Chinese-born executive of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Beijing has denied the spying allegations, made by unnamed US officials in media reports, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive identified as Jensen Huang’s ex-romantic partner, has not publicly commented on the claims.
Late on Monday, the US Commerce Department and the Department of Justice publicly confirmed that investigators had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, leading BIS officials to conduct an on-site inspection of the Singapore-based company and to interview Alice Huang the following year, the statement said.
The Justice Department subsequently took the “lead role” in the criminal investigation, according to the statement.
“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” it said.
US tech stocks fell sharply on Monday as investors weighed the scandal’s fallout on the AI rollout.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5 percent, closing in the red for the third consecutive session.
The broader S&P 500 dropped 1.9 percent.
Shares of Nvidia, which have shed more than 30 percent of their market value over the past month, dropped 4.1 percent.
The other six companies of the “Magnificent Seven” also lost ground, with Alphabet and Amazon seeing the next-biggest declines of 4.1 percent and 3.3 percent, respectively.
The sell-off continued in Asia on Tuesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong closing in the red.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi closed down 1.3 percent and 2.6 percent, respectively, while the Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong dropped 0.9 percent.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, CNBC reports
articles.title_zh: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, CNBC reports
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures are mixed after Nvidia pressures tech to start the week: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures are mixed after Nvidia pressures tech to start the week: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stock futures were mixed early Tuesday, following a losing session as Nvidia weighed on the tech sector.
S&P 500 futures were flat, Dow Jones Industrial Average futures fell 0.32%, while Nasdaq-100 futures gained 0.21%.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 1.34% to close at 58,860.43, while the Topix lost 1.57% to 3,840.02.South Korea's Kospi dropped 2.59% to 4,968.48, while the small-cap Kosdaq declined 2.34% to 650.06. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 closed 1.79% lower at 8883.20.
Mainland China's CSI 300 slipped 0.08% to 3,976.46, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index fell 1.03% as of its last hour of trade.
In regular U.S. trading Monday, Nvidia shares pulled back 4.1%, as traders dumped the chipmaker ahead of its fiscal third-quarter report, due Tuesday after the bell. Other stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade fell as well, including AMD, Micron Technology and Sandisk.
"The tape feels increasingly fragile as Nvidia's AI premium continues to unwind and investors reassess the durability of the ecosystem built around its dominance," said Ben Emons, founder of FedWatch Advisors, in a note. "This backdrop has fueled the 'dispersion trade,' gradually eroding the extreme concentration that has defined the S&P 500 and Nasdaq."
Nvidia has been tumbling since last week. Jensen Huang resigned from the CEO post Thursday after reports emerged that he had multiple affairs , including one with an alleged Chinese spy . Further, the chipmaker's board of directors is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The stock has dropped almost 24% this month, putting it on pace for its biggest monthly decline since April 2022 — when it plunged 32%.
The 30-stock Dow on Monday slid more than 700 points, or 1.4%, while the S&P 500 lost 1.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.5%, its biggest one-day decline since Nov. 5.
On Tuesday, investors will pore through a slew of economic data, including October retail sales and import prices. On the earnings front, Disney and Home Depot are set to report before the opening bell.
Asia-Pacific markets closed lower Tuesday, with South Korea's Kospi leading losses in the region.
Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 1.34% to close at 58,860.43, while the Topix lost 1.57% to 3,840.02.
South Korea's Kospi dropped 2.59% to 4,968.48, while the small-cap Kosdaq declined 2.34% to 650.06.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 closed 1.79% lower at 8,883.20
Mainland China's CSI 300 ended flat at 3,976.46, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was down 1.03% as of its last hour of trade.
Deutsche Bank shares opened 6% lower after numerous media outlets, including the Financial Times , Der Spiegel and Le Monde , published findings from a huge tranche of leaked internal documents revealing how the lender grappled with its problematic clients and assets after CEO Christian Sewing took over in 2018.
Emails and sensitive documents show how the bank dealt with years of scandals, which led to billions in fines and legal costs. New information includes that the lender processed almost $600 million in "suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein," according to the FT's report.
Deutsche Bank told CNBC in a statement: "The matters which are in focus of the media reports date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades. Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators."
"In recent years our bank has gone through a fundamental transformation including 7 billion euros of investments in our control environment between 2019-2025. Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters."
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
U.K. workers' average earnings grew by 3.5% annually in the July to September period, the Office for National Statistics said Tuesday , slowing from 3.7% in the three months to August.
Economists polled by Reuters expected growth of 3.6%.
The U.K. employment rate rose 0.3 percentage points quarter-on-quarter and 0.4 percentage points year-on-year, hitting 75.4%.
Money market pricing suggested around a 90% chance of a quarter-point interest rate hike by the Bank of England at its December meeting, according to LSEG data on Tuesday morning.
BOE Governor Andrew Bailey told CNBC earlier this month that the central bank was "not currently seeing strong pass-through into inflation in other parts of the economy" from the recent energy price shock and would monitor the situation following its November rate hike .
"Coupled with recent GDP figures showing the UK economy was relatively resilient in the third quarter, today's data will likely give policymakers greater confidence that the economy could withstand another interest rate rise in December. Much will now depend on Wednesday's inflation reading," Kit Rees, investment strategist at Quilter, said by email.
Oil prices fell Tuesday as expectations of a global supply surplus outweighed concerns over continued attacks on energy infrastructure and shipping in the Middle East.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude fell 0.71% to $92.44 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures declined 0.69% to $85.72 a barrel.
The International Energy Agency said Friday that the global oil market was expected to return to a surplus in the fourth quarter, as Middle East exports recover faster than demand.
Meanwhile, oil cartel OPEC met virtually on Monday to review members' maximum sustainable production capacity, a measure used to help determine future output quotas. The broader OPEC+ alliance, which includes Russia, is scheduled to meet Nov. 29 to discuss production policy for 2027.
Shares of Chinese internet search engine Baidu fell 6.25% in Hong Kong on Tuesday after the company reported a 1% year-over-year decline in third-quarter revenue to 30.8 billion yuan ($4.6 billion).
Baidu's online marketing services revenue dropped 22% from a year earlier to 11.9 billion yuan, while its revenue from its AI cloud infrastructure business surged 94%.
The company's U.S.-listed shares closed 5.37% lower on Monday.
Major Asian technology stocks fell on Tuesday after Nvidia shares extended losses in U.S. after hours trading, as uncertainty persisted over the chipmaker's leadership following Jensen Huang's departure. Nvidia is searching for a new CEO, while a petition calling for Huang's reinstatement has garnered more than 180,000 signatures.
Japan's SoftBank Group dropped 4.68% in early trading.
In South Korea, Nvidia suppliers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics fell 1.52% and 2.34%, respectively, dragging down the benchmark Kospi index.
Asia-Pacific markets opened lower on Tuesday.
Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 0.76%, while the Topix declined 1.06%. South Korea's Kospi dropped 1.57%, and the small-cap Kosdaq lost 0.62%.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 1.37%.
Asia-Pacific markets were set to fall Tuesday, tracking sharp declines in U.S. equity benchmarks overnight.
Futures for Japan's Nikkei 225 in Chicago were at 59,075 while in Osaka they were last at 59,200, compared with the index's previous close of 59,662.02.
Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 23,669 compared with the index's last close of 23,753.84.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 1.30% in early trade.
Wall Street's big bets came into view on Monday, as major investors released their latest 13F filings, which show where they put their money to work by the end of the third quarter.

articles.title_orig: Trump Backs Huang Comeback While Nvidia Board Seeks New CEO
articles.title_zh: Trump Backs Huang Comeback While Nvidia Board Seeks New CEO
articles.content_orig:
Even after a decade of wrecking-ball politics, President Donald Trump somehow still conjures eye-popping moments.
His insouciance on Monday over the possibility that his associate and AI trailblazer Jensen Huang might have walked into a Chinese intelligence trap was stunning coming from the commander in chief.
“China plays games with us, and we play games with China,” Trump said.
Huang, frequently at the president’s side as he charted the government’s AI policy , was toppled as CEO of Nvidia after reports of several affairs, including one with a woman US officials flagged as a possible Chinese asset.
This is more than a regular corporate scandal. Nvidia is vital to America’s AI ​ rivalry with China , which Trump says will determine which country wins the superpower race. Nvidia chips are deeply embedded in multiple US military applications and will be vital to forging a US edge in the new frontier of 21st-century warfare.
So the risks of any compromise of Huang would be considerable, even if Trump and Vice President JD Vance insisted Monday that it wasn’t clear if the woman, Alice Huang (no relation), was a spy. China has denied the reports.
Trump rationalized the situation as only he could. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” he told reporters as he left for an Asia trip that, with ironic timing, will bring him face-to-face with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week.
The most immediate red flag is over national security.
CNN and other outlets have reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Trump on Huang’s possible exposure on an earlier trip to China. But Trump insisted Monday, “I haven’t heard that.”
If he was being truthful, his reply raised questions about whether the White House acted with sufficient urgency to inform the president about a possible espionage threat so close to his inner circle.
A graver question awaits if it emerges that Trump was informed but continued to appear in public and consult with Nvidia’s then-CEO.
Trump’s presidency is unique in that policies and government actions often seem to spring not from an organized policy process but his own idiosyncratic character and experience.
During his two terms, Trump has sometimes shrugged off inconvenient facts that would interfere with his priorities. This may explain his blasé reaction to the Huang scandal. But the president is not simply defending his associate. On Monday, he added his voice to a growing Silicon Valley campaign for Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia that is also backed by Elon Musk and some 180,000 other signatories.
Nvidia’s board indicated Monday it was not mulling a return for Huang. The tech analyst Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote on X that “the old Jensen with the black leather jacket and rock star persona is gone for good” and that any return would be “ridiculous in our view given the legal/Board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles.”
Despite such complications, Trump insisted that Huang’s return “certainly isn’t a bad idea” since he’d “learned a big lesson.”
One explanation could be that Huang’s embarrassment has echoes in the president’s own life and experience. Trump has often given the impression that he believes that powerful, wealthy men do not have to live by the same rules and moral codes that constrain others. “When you’re a star, they let you do it, you can do anything,” Trump was caught saying in lewd remarks about women on a 2005 “Access Hollywood” tape leaked in 2016.
That scandal at first seemed destined to end his political career short of the White House. But it instead showcased the superpower that would long sustain him — impunity.
On Monday, Trump noted the personal implications of Huang’s plight saying, “He has the family situation, which is a rough deal.” His implication, however, was that such behavior — which also allegedly included an affair with a company subordinate, according to the New York Times — should not disqualify Huang from the role.
But the president’s distaste for the consequences that come with personal indiscretions is not the only possible reason to back Huang’s restoration.
Nvidia is the central tent pole in the entire US AI industry. Huang has been an inspirational leader who also seeded many other companies in the sector with cash and lending. The chip king is about as close to irreplaceable as it’s possible to get. “Even heroes have flaws,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said at a Semafor event on Monday, though he wouldn’t say if Huang should return to Nvidia.
But the most critical reason for Trump’s support may lie in an important new global shift.
Huang is one of a select breed of superstar AI oligarchs whose products, wealth and power have made them hugely powerful non-state actors in the great game of geopolitics. No one elected them or can hold them to account, but their revolutionary technologies are changing life on the planet.
The implications are vast. Interruptions to the military version of the Starlink internet system , for instance, recently curtailed Ukraine’s operations against Russia. And they raised this conundrum: Will it soon be possible for any nation to fight a war without the cooperation of the service’s owner, Elon Musk?
Huang’s company is also deeply entwined with the fate of the US economy. Nvidia is America’s second most valuable firm and helped power the AI stock-market gold rush of the first two years of Trump’s second term. But the company’s stock has been on a downward slide over the scandal.
The consequences for the US economy and Trump’s already diminished presidency and legacy would be incalculable if the company’s crisis pulled the broader stock market down with it.
CNN has also reported that the president’s holdings have included Nvidia stock . The White House has denied that Trump benefited financially from his time in office, stressing that he does not conduct his own trades and that his investments are overseen by outside managers.
The Nvidia drama is beginning to look like one of those long-running Washington storms that inexorably widen.
It’s already dragged the president into the position of defending a disgraced executive, which only encourages headlines about a possible espionage drama close to the White House.
Now, the affair has ignited a feud inside his Cabinet between Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who accused his colleague last week of failing to block China from obtaining Nvidia AI chips.
The president’s ambivalent response to the quarrel on Monday will only fuel impressions of a leadership vacuum inside his administration. It was also a fresh and glaring contradiction of the core principle of his AI policy — beating Beijing.
“One view is you don’t want to insult China. We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them,” Trump said. “And the other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do. I can’t say either is wrong or right. We’ll let you know.”
The president’s vague answers as the Nvidia scandal grows will also increase the appetite of Democratic investigators who are salivating at the chance to use their new majorities to probe alleged West Wing corruption.
But ultimately, the Huang scandal poses a more existential question. Is the epochal power of AI growing so indispensable to US strategic goals and national security that its creators are becoming indispensable no matter what they do?

articles.title_orig: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.title_zh: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.content_orig:
The Justice and Commerce Departments announced late Monday that they were pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore company once led by a woman whom U.S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive.
The announcement appeared to be an effort to counter criticism that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was slow to investigate Megaspeed. It has become the most prominent example of companies that American authorities believe are skirting export rules on the powerful artificial intelligence chips made by Nvidia, the world’s leading manufacturer.
Nvidia exports have exposed a rift in the Trump administration between officials who believe American A.I. technology needs to be kept out of China for national security reasons and others who want a more hands-off approach to export controls.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a TV interview on Friday that his department had been pushing for months to add Megaspeed to a trade blacklist, but that the Commerce Department “holds the pen.”
“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.
That the Justice Department was included in the Monday night announcement appeared to add heft to the investigation’s importance and signaled to critics that administration officials did not intend to ignore the issue.
Megaspeed was created and led for a time by Alice Huang, who U.S. officials say was an asset for Chinese intelligence. The New York Times reported last year that she and Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had a close relationship, and last week Mr. Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife with Ms. Huang.

articles.title_orig: The Death of ‘Keep 1.5 Alive’
articles.title_zh: The Death of ‘Keep 1.5 Alive’
articles.content_orig:
There was a reason, 11 years ago in Paris, that world leaders set themselves a target to keep the global rise in temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius compared with preindustrial levels. Beyond that, climate scientists say, warming will dangerously change our way of life.
We got a taste of it this year, as temperatures rose above the threshold for several months. Heat waves. Wildfires. Flash floods. And with a super El Niño year unfolding, next year might be worse. As one climate expert put it to me: This El Niño will effectively offer a time machine to the 2030s, showing what will happen if we don’t radically cut carbon emissions.
My colleague David Gelles, host of the Climate Forward newsletter, has been following the much diminished U.N. climate talks in Turkey. Today he writes about the death of 1.5 degrees and what that means for the planet.
It was the climate movement’s unifying slogan for the past decade: “Keep 1.5 Alive.”
The tagline referred to the central ambition of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: US presses UN agency over Taiwan flight restrictions, China hits back
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: US presses UN agency over Taiwan flight restrictions, China hits back
articles.content_orig:
Former Seychelles president Wavel Ramkalawan on Thursday said that his government’s last-minute revocation of overflight permission in April for President William Lai’s (賴清德) chartered aircraft en route to Eswatini was wrong and should never happen again.
“This [the decision] was totally wrong. And this is why I stood up, and the leader of the opposition also stood up to condemn that decision. And I hope this doesn’t happen again,” Ramkalawan said in an interview in Taipei.
Ramkalawan was in Taiwan mainly to attend Liberal International’s 65th Congress in Taipei. He is an Anglican priest who served as president of Seychelles from 2020 to last year.
Lai had originally been scheduled to travel to Eswatini on April 22. The trip was suspended after Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar abruptly revoked overflight clearance for his chartered aircraft.
Taiwan accused China of being behind the moves by the three Indian Ocean island countries. The foreign ministries of Seychelles and Madagascar said they had rescinded the overflight permissions in accordance with their “one China” policy.
Taiwan subsequently rescheduled the trip, and Lai visited the African kingdom from May 2 to 4 aboard King Mswati III’s aircraft.
After his government made the decision in April, Ramkalawan issued a statement condemning it.
“Seychelles has a long-established commercial relationship with Taiwan based on fishing agreements which have been beneficial to our country,” the April 27 statement said.
“Its citizens have been free to enter or transit through our territorial waters and airspace. Overflight permission to the Taiwanese President should not be an issue in our relationship with China,” he said.
Asked about the statement, Ramkalawan said his country should respect international aviation protocols, adding that “to allow a plane to fly in the airspace should never be considered political. Whoever is on the plane.”
He added that Lai was set to make “a friendly visit to a friendly country” and that Seychelles’ Civil Aviation Authority had already given the go-ahead.
“And it was the president [Patrick Herminie] who admitted in a press conference that he himself intervened to say no, to cancel,” he said.
At a news conference on May 7, Herminie said that Seychelles remained committed to the “one China policy” and did not recognize Taiwan as a sovereign state, a report by the English-language Seychelles News Agency said.
Herminie said he had been briefed on the matter and had requested the cancellation of the overflight authorization, the report said.
Ramkalawan said the incident “has put Seychelles in a bad light.”
“Because it shows that Seychelles is not respecting the ICAO’s international standards, but rather using politics for whatever reason to interfere,” he said, referring to the International Civil Aviation Organization.
Asked whether he believed China was behind the last-minute cancellation of the overflight permit, Ramkalawan said that he did.
“It’s obvious, and I believe that China was also behind the decision of Mauritius and Madagascar,” he said.
He added that he had been warned by the Chinese embassy before traveling to Taiwan for the conference.
“I make it clear. I am not under the thumb of any country. I make my decisions,” he said.
Asked about future cooperation between Taiwan and Seychelles, the former president praised Taiwan for its leadership in semiconductors and many other sectors, including fisheries.
“And you are contributing to the world’s economy, to the prosperity of all nations of the world. So, therefore, because we’re talking about development, Taiwan should be considered a partner, and that’s the way I see it,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Trump Won’t Just Be Late to a Southeast Asia Summit. He’ll Be Really Late.
articles.title_zh: Trump Won’t Just Be Late to a Southeast Asia Summit. He’ll Be Really Late.
articles.content_orig:
For the second year in a row, President Trump is attending the annual gathering of Southeast Asian leaders, a show of alliance to a region that the United States sees as a strategic and maritime counterweight to China.
But Mr. Trump will reach the gathering, held this year in Manila, only on Tuesday, just as the summit wraps up, and he is not expected to make any significant policies or diplomacy moves.
Mixed signals like this — to say nothing of Mr. Trump’s punishing tariffs — are adding to a widespread belief within ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, that the United States is not a reliable partner. That leaves the bloc balancing between Washington and Beijing, with which many of its members have deep trade partnerships.
“They’ve learned that the United States is not reliable, so a lot of the hedging has been away from the United States,” said Ted Osius, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam.
The Philippines, America’s oldest security ally in Asia, provides a window into this balancing act.
After taking office three years ago, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. reversed his predecessor’s tilt toward China and pivoted back toward the United States. That stance contributed to many tense encounters between Filipino and Chinese vessels in the South China Sea, where Manila and Beijing have competing territorial claims.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
articles.title_zh: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
US president Donald Trump heads to Asia this week to take part in back-to-back summits on economic cooperation, world conflicts, and nuclear weapons.
Much of the world’s focus will be on the historic, first-ever trilateral meeting between Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday.
However, hours before leaving the White House for the Philippines, Trump managed to raise the stakes even further while suggesting North Korean leader could also join them.
“(Xi) was here a month ago, and we're also going to meet with (Russian) President Putin, and we may meet with Kim Jong Un also,” Trump said.
“So that'll be good. We have a chance to accomplish a lot.,” while stressing the decision on Kim’s attendance was up to Beijing.
Despite the strategic importance of the issues on the agenda during the trip, it could still be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal.
CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign last week after it emerged he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The ousted tech boss has close ties to the US president, even accompanying him on Air Force One during his last trip to China in May.
However Trump is not expected to directly raise the spy allegations with Xi, one senior US administration told Reuters on condition of anonymity.
The US president is due tol land in Manila on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit, before flying to Shenzhen in southern China late on Wednesday for the two-day Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum, at the end of which the first-ever three-way discussion between Xi, Trump, and ‌Putin will take place.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” said a White House spokesperson.
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February. It is the first time since the early 1970s that there is no legally binding limits on US and Russian nuclear forces without another agreement being under negotiation.
Russia and the US possess the largest nuclear arsenal in the world, followed by China.
The United Nations has long urged for nuclear disarmament, warning that rising geopolitical tensions have fuelled nuclear risks around the world.
“If there is a denuclearisation program, we are ready to be fully engaged in that and contribute to make it a success,” UN ​Secretary-General Antonio ‌Guterres said on Monday in Manila, where he is attending the Asean summit.
The denuclearisation talks will also spotlight the war in Iran, with Tehran being a strategic partner of both China and Russia.
Leaders at Asean are likely to renew calls for peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including in the South China Sea and in Myanmar. They are expected to push for efforts to protect their economies and citizens from the continuing fallout from global conflicts, such as the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf.
The White House has said that Trump plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand while in Manila, while US officials will also meet on the sidelines with the so-called Quad, or Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, which consists of Australia, India, Japan and the US.
Trump will be looking for an overseas success on the trip, following the disastrous midterm results that saw his Republican party lose control of Congress.
“The president will undoubtedly be seeking to use this trip to reassert leadership, authority, demonstrate his statesmanship capabilities and essentially show off on the international stage,” Kurt Tong, a former US ambassador for Apec, told Bloomberg.
The US president will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday.
But expectations for progress at the talks in China are not high. No agreement is expected afterward, a senior US official said, according to AP and Reuters.
“In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi,” US-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling told PBS News .
“With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises,” he said.
Other critical issues at these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition.

articles.title_orig: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
articles.title_zh: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
articles.content_orig:
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko at the site of a missile strike in October
Two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital have reportedly been struck in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The missiles hit Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges spanning the Dnipro River, Klitschko said, adding that water and power supplies had been disrupted.
Meanwhile, Ukraine struck the landmark Kerch Bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea killing two people, the region's Moscow-installed governor said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky had earlier warned that Moscow might launch further strikes on the country on Monday night, after Ukrainian, US and European officials held further talks aimed at ending the years-long conflict.
Those online talks, attended by US envoy Jared Kushner and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, came after Russia said it recorded the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems".
"Some areas are experiencing disruptions to water and heating supplies", he added.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services have been damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Residents of Kyiv typically shelter in the city's underground stations during air raids.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv. An estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Several of the capital's major bridges were also targeted by Russian drone strikes in October .
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.
Separately, the Ukrainian military struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea for a second consecutive day , the region's Moscow-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov said on Telegram.
Traffic across the bridge had been suspended, he added.
The landmark bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014.
Russian President Vladimir Putin inaugurated the bridge to great fanfare in 2018. The severity of the latest strike on Kerch Bridge is still unclear, though it is protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.
Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.
The latest round of tit-for-tat strikes came after US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks on ways to facilitate "direct engagement" between Russia and Europe to end the war.
Following Monday's meeting, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, said the US was committed to providing Ukraine with a "strong, credible security guarantees", as well as a path towards EU membership.
He added that Nato "will remain a critical pillar of European security", and that preparations are underway for a further multilateral meeting "in the near future".
In an address on Monday evening, Zelensky said that the meeting was "difficult", adding that more needed to be done to support Ukraine's defence against Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Zelensky said that Europe was represented for the first time by the full delegation that will participate in negotiations with Moscow - including the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the EU and Nato.
The Ukrainian president has long called for European delegates to be included in any peace talks, which he argues is necessary because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
He also said that Moscow is receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials said that the final death toll from a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian village of Kamyshuvakha earlier this month had reached 72.
Four people are still considered missing after the bombing, which Ukrainian officials say is one of the deadliest individual attacks since the start of the war in 2022.
Footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, showed residents going to an underground shelter after the initial attack on 2 November. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
Ukrainian police said of those killed were police officers, "staff of the gymnasium, utility workers and medical personnel".
Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title_orig: What we know about what caused the FAA's nationwide ground stop
articles.title_zh: What we know about what caused the FAA's nationwide ground stop
articles.content_orig:
Airports were thrown into chaos, with hundreds of flights canceled and thousands of travelers stranded. A Federal Aviation Administration investigation soon traced the disaster to an unlikely source: A router that had locked up the nation’s air traffic control network.
That incident happened 17 years ago – leading to urgent calls for FAA upgrades.
Yet on Friday, an eerily similar scene played out, this time with a rare nationwide halt to all flights as communications with pilots broke down.
Once again, the FAA now suspects the problems began with a single router, newly installed in a remote radio outpost in Arkansas.
While federal investigators with the FBI and FAA are still working to untangle exactly what went wrong last week – and who is to blame – the similar 2009 incident is a startling illustration of how long US officials have battled to upgrade an aging flight control network.
A CNN review of government oversight reports and past incidents vividly shows how decades of warnings about the FAA’s aging infrastructure have failed to head off the kind of mass outages that again struck America’s aviation industry on Friday.
“We’ve known the system has been antiquated for many years,” said Margaret Wallace, an assistant professor of aviation management at the Florida Institute of Technology. “Much of what was there can almost date back to World War II.”
The Trump administration has touted its plans to speedily replace antiquated copper wiring with fiber optics and newer equipment and pointed to Friday’s outage as evidence that Congress needs to provide more than the $12.5 billion already earmarked for upgrades.
“Congress did give me $12.5 billion, but they were very specific on how we spend it,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Sunday . “I have no money for a new network. I don’t have any new money to build new software to separate planes in the air space.”
But Friday’s incident, which Duffy said occurred during one of those upgrades, has also sharpened questions about how effectively the administration and its key contractors are carrying out the improvements already in progress.
Similar concerns were raised in September in a US Government Accountability Office report warning the FAA could potentially cause more breakdowns by moving too hastily in efforts to modernize its systems.
The report stated the FAA had made progress in replacing thousands of old copper wires with high-speed fiber optic cables but also expressed concern that the agency had not effectively scheduled those replacements to “reduce impacts to controller operations.”
“FAA could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions,” stated the GAO report , which added, “If these risks are realized, FAA would need to continue to rely on severely outdated systems that are prone to failure leading to more flight delays and safety incidents.”
The infrastructure that keeps thousands of flights safely separated in US airspace is built on a network of comparatively ancient technology – from copper phone lines to old computers, all of which must link a complex nationwide network of air traffic controllers.
Government officials have long sounded alarms about breakdowns in that system, which at times has failed spectacularly.
In 2009, an FAA telecommunications outage affected more than 100 air traffic facilities and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide.
A review by the Department of Transportation’s inspector general later found a technician had “incorrectly configured” a router, which caused an improper flow of air traffic data that blocked much of the system.
The technician described in the IG’s report worked for Harris Corporation, which later merged with another business to form L3Harris, the contractor now under scrutiny for the latest outage.
An FAA review panel later recommended a spate of improvements in the wake of that mass outage, including looking into setting up new backup systems.
Eight years later, though, the FAA’s inspector general warned that technology disruptions were still a major threat to the nation’s air travel – citing a number of other recent failures, including a fire in Chicago and a flood in Texas that disabled control towers for long periods of time.
“Significant work remains to mitigate the impact of air traffic control disruptions,” the 2017 report found .
In 2023, the FAA briefly halted all domestic flight departures after another  outage. A subsequent GAO report found many air traffic control systems were increasingly prone to failures and relied on hard-to-find spare parts.
The assessment determined that more than a third of the systems were “unsustainable,” with others heading in the same direction. That same year, a safety review team explicitly warned of potential communication failures due to aging infrastructure and budgetary constraints, telling the FAA in a report that “risk could quickly reach unacceptable levels.”
Last year, a series of disruptions prompted more scrutiny. Outages at a Philadelphia control facility caused the FAA to halt flights at Newark Liberty International Airport. A controller who spoke with CNN anonymously at the time said a single data feed connecting two facilities – similar to an extension cord-like line – had crashed at least twice.
Following the outages, federal investigators questioned whether the FAA had adequately assessed the reliability of telecommunications lines before relocating Newark’s airspace management from New York to Philadelphia. An IG report described a “burnt copper wire” and “failures of both primary and redundant communication infrastructure.”
President Donald Trump’s mega-spending bill passed by Republicans last year included $12.5 billion to start widespread upgrades to the FAA’s infrastructure, a plan Duffy touted at an aviation summit in April.
He said half of the system’s old wires had already been replaced. He referenced the incidents in Newark and blamed outdated wires, stating that since those had been replaced Newark had some of the “most on-time performance.”
“In one year, this administration has done more in replacing old wires than the last administration did in all four of their years,” Duffy told the audience.
Yet the GAO’s September report struck a more cautious note about those plans and criticized the FAA for not having detailed cost estimate and integration plans around its new air traffic control system.
Without doing so, it would “increase the likelihood of FAA repeating its history of cost overruns, delays, and unmet performance targets,” the report found.
The latest mass outage to America’s air traffic control system began as a result of implementing those new upgrades, officials now believe.
Duffy said at a news conference that L3Harris was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from copper wires to fiber optics prior to the outage.
After the contractor installed a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas, the device started pinging the FAA networks at a rapid rate on Friday afternoon, according to an FAA statement. A second router in Texas experienced similar issues. The FAA disabled both routers and approximately 60 others as a precaution.
The FAA says that during the outage, 17 of its 22 air route traffic control centers experienced problems.
A telecommunications router suspected of playing a role in the disruption has been sent to a testing facility in Florida, according to a senior administration official.
The FAA and L3Harris are investigating whether the failure was caused by a defective router or an installation or configuration error. The FBI is also involved out of an abundance of caution, the official said.
In a statement, L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA’s investigation and noted the company had already completed more than 70% of the conversion from copper wires to fiber optics.

articles.title_orig: Major banking outage linked to Chase, impacted Wells Fargo and BofA
articles.title_zh: Major banking outage linked to Chase, impacted Wells Fargo and BofA
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of customers across the United States reported problems accessing banking services and making payments after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted transactions involving other banks.
The problems on Monday affected customers at several major financial institutions, including Wells Fargo and Bank of America, while some users also reported delays with Zelle payments.
So, what caused the US bank outages, which banks were affected, and have services returned to normal?
Thousands of US customers reported problems accessing online banking services after JPMorgan Chase said a software issue caused knock-on effects for transactions involving other banks.
The disruption extended to customers of at least five other banks, who reported issues accessing services and completing transactions.
According to the French news agency AFP, reports on outage-tracking Downdetector peaked at around 2pm Eastern Standard Time (19:00 GMT) before declining later in the day.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system – it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesperson for the bank.
Customers of several major US banks reported problems on Monday.
These included JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, US Bank, Truist and Capital One.
However, not all the banks reported problems with their own systems.
Chase confirmed experiencing technical problems, while US Bank said its own systems were not directly affected. Capital One and Truist also said their services were operating normally.
JPMorgan Chase said that a software bug in its internal hardware systems had slowed transaction processing and may have delayed transactions involving other banks.
Some customers said they were not able to access accounts and funds, although Chase said customers continued to have access.
The bank stressed that the disruption was not systemic and that other banks may have experienced delays when processing transactions involving Chase.
Chase is the consumer banking division of JPMorgan Chase, which holds the most assets of any US bank. It handles payments involving other financial institutions, meaning a technical problem at Chase can also delay transactions for customers at other banks, even if those banks’ systems are operating normally.
“This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” Evangelisti added.
Zelle is the peer-to-peer third-party payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed.
It is owned by Early Warning Services, an Arizona-based company that is itself owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.
In the US, some customers also reported problems sending and receiving payments through Zelle.
However, Zelle said its network was operating normally.
The company said that customers access Zelle through participating banks and credit unions so technical problems at those institutions can affect the ability to make a payment even if Zelle’s own systems are fully operational.
US Bank said its systems were not directly affected but warned that customers sending or receiving Zelle payments involving other financial institutions could experience delays.
JPMorgan Chase said that transactions were processing normally again following the disruption.
A Chase spokesperson said that shortly after close of business on Monday, at approximately 6:30pm (23:30 GMT), transactions were posting normally, according to NBC News.
However, the restoration of Chase’s transaction processing does not necessarily mean every delayed payment has been completed.
There is no confirmed connection between Monday’s outages and the recent Microsoft outage and disruptions impacting the US government’s transport agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
The banking problems followed two major incidents in the US last week.
On Thursday, Microsoft experienced a widespread outage that disrupted services including Outlook. A day later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop following a technical failure affecting air traffic control communications.
The incidents had different reported causes. JPMorgan Chase said its disruption was due to a software bug, while the FAA disruption involved malfunctioning equipment.
However, Jody Westby, CEO of cybersecurity advisory firm Global Cyber Risk, told Al Jazeera that the series of incidents raised questions about the reliability and security of critical infrastructure.
“I think it’s very concerning that everyone’s just jumping to the conclusion it’s a technical issue, it’s a software bug, it was old equipment,” she said.
“I don’t think that any of that is a complete explanation the public deserves.”
Westby said she believed more detailed investigations were needed.
“My concern is that we are not diligently looking into these incidents and analysing them, and even with a global working group to make sure that we can determine whether there are any correlations.”

articles.title_orig: Top Trump aides to meet with Europeans, Ukrainians on peace plan
articles.title_zh: Top Trump aides to meet with Europeans, Ukrainians on peace plan
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has held new talks with United States and European officials on ending the war with Russia, hours before Kyiv’s mayor reported strikes on two bridges in the capital.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Monday’s online discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and European representatives as “not easy”. But he said participants had agreed to meet in Berlin with the “Coalition of the Willing”, a group of countries supporting Ukraine, as the US and Europe step up peace talks this week.
“Diplomatic processes are actively underway and we hope that these efforts will not be in vain,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
He also warned that Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes that night and throughout Tuesday.
Later on Monday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said preliminary reports indicated that the North and South bridges across the Dnipro River had been hit. Air defence units were operating, and Reuters news agency witnesses heard a series of loud explosions.
Ukraine on Monday struck a key bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defence ministry data indicated was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022. The Crimea Bridge was again struck overnight, with nearly 200 drones intercepted near Moscow, according to Telegram statements.
Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said Washington was making progress towards an agreement in coordination with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.
“Important challenges remain, and a final agreement will require difficult decisions,” he wrote on X.
He said he and Witkoff had also spoken with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov about the next steps. Their discussions included how to arrange direct engagement between Europe and Russia so each could hear the other’s concerns and proposals.
The exchanges followed last week’s talks in Abu Dhabi , where US, Ukrainian and Russian officials met together for the first time in nine months. Those negotiations produced an agreement on a prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war.
Witkoff and Kushner later met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and said European representatives would join the next round. On Monday, Moscow disputed that assertion.
Zelenskyy said representatives from France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Poland had participated fully in Monday’s discussion and would have the same representation in future meetings with Russian negotiators.
Ushakov said Russia had not agreed to expand the talks beyond the existing Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations. No date had been agreed for the next round, he added.
European governments, meanwhile, were preparing their negotiating team while maintaining pressure on Moscow.
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee welcomed renewed talks and the agreement on EU representation following diplomatic meetings in Abu Dhabi and Dublin last week. But she said, “Russia has clearly not changed its position.”
Speaking ahead of Monday’s meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, McEntee said 113 new sanctions on Russia were intended to maintain pressure on Moscow “as it intensified attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure during the winter”.
“We are also working to ensure Ukraine has the finance and the military support it needs while advancing Ukraine’s path to EU membership,” she said.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia wanted a lasting peace rather than a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to recover from the damage inflicted by Russian forces.
He said Moscow sought peace lasting “years, even centuries”, adding that negotiations were complex and could take considerable time.
Separately, Trump said he would discuss the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin in China, saying he believed Putin wanted to end the war.
“I think he’s backing down a little bit,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, I think he’d like to see it finish.”
The planned Berlin meeting would allow Ukraine and its supporters to agree on their next negotiating steps. Russia had yet to accept their proposed representation in the talks that would follow.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration's $50B air traffic demand hits GOP turbulence in the Senate
articles.title_zh: Trump administration's $50B air traffic demand hits GOP turbulence in the Senate
articles.content_orig:
The air traffic control tower at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in Los Angeles, California, on Nov. 14, 2026.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday blamed the previous day’s nationwide ground stop on the replacement of copper wires at a “remote” Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) facility. Installing new fiber optic lines led to critical communication breakdowns, he said.
About 7,500 flights were delayed and over 9,000 were canceled on Friday, according to FlightAware . Some 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. Eastern, shortly after the ground stop began.
The incident raised questions about what might have led to the historic event—only the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11—and what authorities were doing to prevent it from happening again.
“What we’re working to determine is whether we had incompetence,” Duffy said Saturday, which saw nearly 6,000 additional flights canceled. "Or did they install a faulty router?"
As investigators continued working to pinpoint the source of the problem, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters in Washington, D.C., that disrupted flight schedules were expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday and promised that the “worst is behind us.”
While that may be true for this specific outage, Duffy warned Friday that what happened was not an isolated incident and said that outages would likely continue to occur until antiquated communications equipment across the FAA’s air traffic control network was brought up to date.
“It was the old legacy equipment. It failed,” Duffy said. “And listen, it’s going to continue to fail.”
The Transportation Secretary went on to call for Congress to provide $50 billion before the end of the year to upgrade air traffic control and airport infrastructure, increasing the administration’s recent $30.1 billion request, which included $10.1 billion specifically for air traffic control modernization.
President Donald Trump addressed the outage for the first time on Sunday, urging Congress to approve additional funding in a post on Truth Social . “If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” he said.
There is reason to believe, however, that financial support alone will not solve the problems currently faced by the FAA. Those include shortages in fully certified air traffic controllers, weaknesses in planning and coordinating necessary modernization work, and vulnerabilities to cybersecurity threats.
TIME has reached out to Duffy’s office for comment.
Modernizing the FAA’s air traffic control system has been a goal of the industry for years, says Edward Booth, an aviation attorney and pilot based in Jacksonville, and billions of dollars have already been sunk into the process.
“There has been a very methodical four-part, four-stage plan to upgrade that,” Booth tells TIME, referencing NextGen , a multibillion-dollar FAA modernization initiative dating to 2003. It has included shifting toward satellite-based aircraft tracking, digital communications, and more efficient flight routes.
Booth says a major focus of those earlier modernization efforts was making more efficient use of airspace.
“They have tried to squeeze more airplanes into limited space, make better use of the limited runways available in the system, and they started with completely changing the way airplanes are tracked in the world. It's a world standard now,” he says, pointing to how NextGen has already made strides in air travel.
The agency’s newer overhaul builds on earlier modernization work and includes replacing aging communications equipment, radar, and other infrastructure, with its first phase targeted for completion by the end of 2028.
“It's a very highly technical, robust system,” Booth says of the National Airspace System (NAS), “but it seems the weak spot was discovered yesterday afternoon.”
For more than two decades, the FAA has been working to modernize the NAS while fighting an uphill battle against aging infrastructure. The average U.S. air traffic control tower was 40 years old, and most radar systems were approaching that age, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Chairman Sam Graves wrote in a May 2025 op-ed .
Congress had already ordered an independent review of the FAA’s aging technology: The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required an audit of legacy systems deployed before 2000—including their vulnerability to single-point failures—and a plan to accelerate replacement or improvement of those found to pose risks. In a written response to Congress , the FAA said that nonprofit research organization MITRE completed the audit in August 2025. The response said the findings would guide modernization efforts, but did not disclose the specific findings or resulting actions.
In July 2025, Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA to upgrade its “radar, software, hardware, and telecommunications” at more than 4,600 sites through December 2028.
As of Nov. 5, the FAA said it has “replaced 69% of copper wires, installed Surface Awareness Initiative (SAI) systems at 143 towers, transitioned 26 towers to electronic flight strips [and] installed 226 IP Voice Switches.”
The updates were noted within an announcement saying the FAA was beginning to phase out the floppy disks used in air traffic control. It said that it had launched a replacement system that would include a digital display board with data about disruptions, weather conditions, and advisories. The announcement identified five initial facilities and set a goal of installing the system at 435 sites by the end of 2028.
Duffy called these efforts “the latest signal that America’s brand new air traffic control system is coming at lightning speed.”
The FAA then announced Nov. 10 that it was expanding its AI-powered scheduling and flight-planning tool—known as SMART (Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories)—to airspace managed by all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers nationwide. SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million contract that also covers the agency’s Flow Management Data and Services program.
Duffy said at Friday’s press conference that SMART had nothing to do with the disruption.
Describing Friday's outage, Duffy said a router being replaced as workers switched from copper wiring to fiber-optic connections began flooding other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting communications and some radar feeds. Systems came back online after officials isolated the work at the remote location, he said.
For Booth, the spread of that disruption underscores the need for safeguards that can contain a problem in one part of the FAA’s communications network before it affects the wider system.
“They need a system that is not prone to single-point failures,” he says.
Booth pointed out that legacy systems—often relying on analog lines, decades-old routers, and interconnected regional hubs—lack the fault-tolerant design needed to prevent a local or routine maintenance glitch from cascading nationwide.
“The public probably would be shocked to learn that the way pilots communicate with air traffic control is tantamount to an old-fashioned telephone line,” he says. “You've got 10, sometimes 15 airplanes competing to talk to a single controller-specified frequency.”
Kumar Sokka, the CEO of Acre Security, says a key consideration when upgrading complex systems is whether individual components can fail without disrupting the entire network.
“Can you remove a single point of failure? Are these systems distributed in a way where it's siloed in certain structures where if something fails, not everything fails, right?” asks Sokka.
He says that many industries come up against issues of balancing the high upfront expense of upgrading legacy systems against the severe financial and operational risks of future outages.

articles.title_zh: Study estimates magnitude of US data center pollution as climate talks unveil clean AI pledge
articles.content_orig:

The rapid proliferation of hyperscale data centres (HDCs) in the USA—mainly driven by the adoption of artificial intelligence—has raised concerns about this industry’s carbon footprint. We compiled facility-level information on 403 US hyperscale data centres operating between May 2024 and April 2025 and estimated their electricity consumption, electricity sources and attributable CO 2 emissions. Across facility-load scenarios, these HDCs consumed approximately 68–99 TWh of electricity and were associated with approximately 21–31 million metric tons of CO 2 under a location-based, total-output balancing-authority attribution method. Under the central scenario, HDC electricity demand was approximately 82 TWh, corresponding to about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption, and attributable CO 2 emissions were approximately 25.7 Mt. Roughly 54% of attributed generation was supplied by fossil-fuel sources. The HDC electricity-weighted total-output carbon intensity was approximately 314 gCO 2 kWh −1 , compared with a US total-output average of approximately 348 gCO 2 kWh −1 . Our approach provides a facility-resolved attributional framework for assessing the carbon footprint of hyperscale data centres using plant-level electricity-generation and emissions data.

Access to the restricted facility-level dataset may be considered for approved research collaborations, subject to the underlying data-use agreement, provider authorization and execution of an appropriate data-use agreement. Requests may be directed to the corresponding author. We provide public state- and balancing-authority-level data exports containing the electricity demand, attributable CO 2 emissions, total-output carbon intensity and attributed fuel mix used in the revised analysis. These aggregate exports reflect the central facility-load scenario ( u = 0.58) and the total-output attribution basis used for the headline results. They are available through the public reproducibility repository 46 . The repository exports, rather than the separate visualization interface, constitute the authoritative public data products for the revised analysis. Because the underlying facility data are protected by a data-use agreement, raw facility identifiers, addresses, coordinates and commercially sensitive facility attributes are not publicly released. The complete facility-level map-generation workflow requires authorized access to those inputs. Access to facility-level map coordinates remains subject to provider authorization and the data-use agreement; public aggregate files do not substitute for the restricted facility-level observations. Source data are provided with this paper.
All code used to estimate HDC power capacity, evaluate the capacity model, compute electricity use and emissions, validate public aggregate exports and reproduce manuscript-facing numerical results is publicly available in the public reproducibility repository 46 . A tagged snapshot corresponding to the Round 3 reproducibility materials is available as version v0.3.1-round3-final 47 . The repository contains: (1) the fully specified scikit-learn capacity-model pipeline, including disclosed predictors, preprocessing, effective hyperparameters, software version and evaluation metrics; (2) a non-identifying 403-row synthetic facility fixture with six missing power-capacity values; (3) a deterministic public synthetic split artefact at results/tables/synthetic_validation/splits.json , together with random and grouped validation outputs; (4) REPRO.md , documenting the validation sample, explicit imputation indicator, software versions, restricted-data workflow and emissions-accounting conventions; (5) scripts/reproduce_model.py , which regenerates the public synthetic validation outputs and writes the deterministic split artefact; (vi) the total-output emissions-attribution workflow using EPA eGRID2023 Revision 2; (7) denominator-audit, plant-inventory, public-export, restricted-data and manuscript-output validation scripts and (8) aggregate state- and balancing-authority-level exports used to verify the headline results. The public synthetic and aggregate materials allow external researchers to execute the capacity-model validation workflow, verify the emissions denominator, reproduce headline scenario totals, sum the public regional exports and run the repository tests without access to restricted facility records.

articles.title_orig: Splatoon 3 Version 12.0.0 Announced, Here Are The Full Patch Notes
articles.title_zh: Splatoon 3 Version 12.0.0 Announced, Here Are The Full Patch Notes
articles.content_orig:
Nintendo's team-based squid-shooter Splatoon 3 is still going strong, and this week the title is getting updated to Version 12.0.0 .
This major update will come with changes to multiplayer, including weapon adjustments. There are also changes to Anarchy Battle, X Battles and challenges. Additionally, there are changes to the GameChat feature on Switch 2. Nintendo also notes how its next update after this one will focus on multiplayer game balance .
You can get the full rundown in the official patch notes below ( via Nintendo's official support page ):
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
Sections marked "on Nintendo Switch 2" apply only to Nintendo Switch 2. All other changes apply to both Nintendo Switch 2 and Nintendo Switch.
Made it possible to participate with a friend in traditional X Battles as a group of two.
Added a feature that allows players to open GameChat and invite friends from their group while playing modes with friends, such as battles or Salmon Run.
This update focuses on making changes to matchmaking and multiplayer balance.
For X Battles, we have added a feature to allow players to play as a pair with a friend. The goal of this feature is to expand the range of ways to play, and we will introduce it on a trial basis starting in Chill Season 2026. After we have introduced it, we will comprehensively analyze how these battles are actually played and how the gameplay situation shifts, including for players who are not playing with a friend. Then we will decide whether to continue providing this feature in future seasons.
For Anarchy Battle (Series), we have changed the matchmaking system such that, in exchange for removing the feature allowing players to continue with the same team, matchmaking will now complete more quickly and with less imbalance of skill level and equipped weapons between players and their opponents.
For Challenges, we have changed how Challenge Power is calculated to make it easier to raise Challenge Power the more wins a player has. With this change, between players who would have ended up with about the same Challenge Power under the previous system, the player who attained the greater number of wins will have the higher final Challenge Power.
For multiplayer balance, we made a variety of changes to main, sub, and special weapons, including changes to the flight distance of Blaster shots.
With most weapons, when a player fires while moving, the player's movement speed is added to the shot's speed to a certain extent, resulting in a more natural trajectory. For Blasters, we have minimized the change in shot flight distance caused by this effect, making it easier to maintain an appropriate distance against an opponent’s Blaster.
Among the special weapons, we have changed the Reefslider because, while there is statistically little impact on victories in matches between extremely skilled players, it has a high impact on matches between less skilled players. The intention behind this change is to alleviate that striking difference. By narrowing the area affected by the explosion we have made it so that players cannot reap the maximum benefit without using it at the precise position. On the other hand, we have extended the invulnerability period to make it harder for opponents who used terrain to survive the explosion to counterattack and easier for the player to make follow-up attacks.
For the Tenta Missiles, we have decreased the vulnerability while firing and expanded the area where it is possible to lock on to opponents. As a result, it will now be easier to use, even in situations where opponents are nearby the player. By decreasing the impact interval, it becomes easier to defeat opponents who are slow to dodge, but the duration for which they must keep dodging is reduced.
We have also added a feature for Nintendo Switch 2 that will make it easier to use GameChat.
The next update will focus on changes to multiplayer balance.
If you haven't already played the game on Switch 2, there's a free upgrade available which includes visual improvements and frame rate optimisations for the platform. In some related news, Splatoon Raiders has also received an eShop demo this week!

The Serbian government has formally rejected Jared Kushnerâs $500 million deal to build a Trump-branded luxury hotel in the countryâs capital.
The nationâs Ministry of Construction confirmed in a written response to the Serbian news outlet Insajder on Saturday that the official process for a termination agreement would be finalized early this week, according to the Polish outlet TVP World .
Construction Minister Aleksandra SofronijeviÄ told Insajder that the Serbian government decided to walk away from the deal in August, and that both sides agreed to drop any potential claims against each other.
The bombed Yugoslav Ministry of Defense building in Belgrade.
Medin Halilovic/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images
The proposed development was first announced in 2024 and would have seen a luxury hotel, residence, and casino occupying the site of the former Yugoslav Ministry of Defense headquarters, which was heavily damaged in a 1999 NATO bombing campaign.
Serbiaâs government had agreed to give Kushnerâs private equity firm, Affinity Partners, a 99-year lease on the property.
But the project sparked intense backlash, and even led to a criminal indictment against several top Serbian officials.
