articles.title_zh: Chase customers report widespread online banking problems
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Chase reports an issue that appears to be causing outages to online and in-person banking services
An issue with Chase banking services led to some customers of that institution and others reporting trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds Monday.
The issues appeared to be affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.
“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” Chase said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”
The issues at Chase were caused by a “technical bug, not a cyber issue,” according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
A Zelle representative said that a technical issue on its platform originated with Chase.
“This is a Chase issue,” a Zelle spokesman told NBC News. “You need to speak to them.”
Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.
The outages were the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week.
Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade .
On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade .
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.content_orig:
In the past week, shares of Nvidia ( NVDA -3.96% ) have been in a downward spiral. News that Jensen Huang has resigned as president and CEO and has been involved in multiple affairs, one of which may involve a Chinese spy, has significantly weighed on the company's valuation.
The stock has fallen so sharply that it is now trading at levels it hasn't been at since June of last year. Given how sudden and significant the sell-off has been, many investors are likely worried that there may still be worse to come. Could the tech stock fall to $100?
Image source: Getty Images.
When things are going well for a stock, the temptation is to assume it'll only continue to do well and rise higher. And when things are going poorly, many investors may fear that things will only get worse. Both outlooks, however, can be incredibly irrational. Sooner or later, the excitement or panic fades, and the stock stabilizes and may even end up going in the opposite direction.
Due to its sharp decline, Nvidia's stock is now trading at around 20 times its trailing earnings. And on a forward basis, based on analyst expectations of future earnings, its forward price-to-earnings multiple is just ten. That's an incredibly low valuation given that the S&P 500 average is a forward earnings multiple of 19.
The stock is already heavily discounted , and for a more significant decline to take place, one that takes it to $100, that would likely require there to be much more negative news around the tech business. And there would also likely need to be an all-out crash in the tech sector.
NASDAQ · As of 2:56 PM ET 11/16/26
The last time Nvidia's stock was at around $100 was after the Liberation Day tariffs were announced in April 2025. Global trade uncertainty weighed on not only Nvidia but the markets as a whole, and unless there's that kind of uncertainty and fear rattling the markets once more, I wouldn't expect Nvidia to fall to those levels anytime soon.
Nvidia is already an incredibly cheap-looking stock to buy given how well it has performed in recent years. Waiting for an even lower price could be risky for investors, because the risk is that it may never reach those levels; buying the stock now may be a much better move than holding out hope that it will fall even further.

articles.title_orig: Warsh Says Fed Is Gaming Out How AI Could Reshape Economy
articles.title_zh: Warsh Says Fed Is Gaming Out How AI Could Reshape Economy
articles.content_orig:
[The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.
Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road."
"I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.
In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.
Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.
In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.
At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint."
"After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."
The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.
Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.
Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.
The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

articles.title_orig: Five EU countries unveil plans for Rwanda deportation hub
articles.title_zh: Five EU countries unveil plans for Rwanda deportation hub
articles.content_orig:
Five European countries unveiled plans on Monday to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.
Under the planned scheme — which is still being negotiated with Rwanda — Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands would send people to a center where the migrants could choose to return home, settle or go somewhere else where they had a right to stay, Kigali said.
“I think it will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges of illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told a press conference in Vienna with her Austrian counterpart and ministers from the countries involved.
The five countries have been working towards a deal for a so-called return hub for several months, officials have said — part of a broader push inside the European Union to increase deportation s and curb irregular migration.
With elections approaching in several EU countries, centrist governments have been toughening immigration policies to try to counter growing public support for far-right parties.
In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s.
The plan “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” read the statement from the International Rescue Committee, the Dutch Council for Refugees and other groups.
Although officials say such a hub would only handle about 100 people at a time, the countries championing it say it would send an important signal that they hope will discourage would-be migrants from making the often perilous journey to Europe.
The project follows the approval of the EU’s new Return Regulation, designed to speed up deportations.
The scheme differs from Britain’s abandoned Rwanda deportation plan in that it would only apply to migrants who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain in the European Union, rather than those whose claims are still being processed.
Rwanda has positioned itself as a destination for migrants whom Western countries want to remove, despite longstanding concerns about its own human rights record.
“Under this partnership, Rwanda would provide a second chance to people who no longer have the legal right to remain in the partner countries,” Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said on Monday.
Rwanda was not looking to be paid for the arrangement, but partner countries would meet the cost of relocation and the integration of any who chose to stay in Rwanda, he added.
Veteran President Paul Kagame won praise from Western and regional leaders for helping end Rwanda’s 1994 genocide and rebuilding the East African country into a destination for investment.
However, critics accuse his government of suppressing dissent and supporting rebels alleged to have committed killings, rapes and other abuse in neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo. Rights advocates also point to restrictions on political freedoms and free speech.
Freedom House rates it “Not Free” and cites what it describes as the suppression of political dissent through surveillance, intimidation, arbitrary detention and torture.
“There is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights,” Amnesty International said in a statement on Monday.
The United States last year began transferring migrants to Rwanda under an agreement allowing it to deport up to 250 people.
Britain abandoned its own plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda after it was ruled unlawful by the country’s Supreme Court in 2023. Kigali sought a £50 million ($63.6 million) payment after the UK scheme was scrapped.
During a September visit to Kigali, two European Parliament lawmakers were shown facilities earmarked for Britain’s abandoned scheme that could potentially house migrants transferred from EU countries, including a hotel.

articles.title_orig: 'A beautiful woman': Trump unsure Nvidia CEO had affair with Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: 'A beautiful woman': Trump unsure Nvidia CEO had affair with Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
President Donald Trump said Monday that he would welcome the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia - days after the chipmaker's co-founder was forced out over an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman - and insisted that no one had proven the woman was a spy.
"There's a big group of people that would like him to return," Trump told reporters as he left the White House to travel to Asia ahead of his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin later this week.
“I think having Jensen go back, a lot of people are asking Jensen. They think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea. I recommended Tim Cook, who, as you know, built Apple, I recommended Tim Cook to go and do a job,” Trump continued.
Huang resigned last week after acknowledging an affair with Alice Huang — no relation — a businesswoman that U.S. officials have described as a suspected asset of China's Ministry of State Security.
The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined she had been recruited by the spy agency and tasked with influencing Huang to push Nvidia toward selling Beijing more of its advanced chips. The Times also reported Jensen Huang’s second affair, with a Nvidia subordinate, moved the company’s board to force him out last week.
In the days since, allies of the former Nvidia boss have been attempting to rally support for his return with an online petition that has thus far garnered more than 100,000 signatures, including from Nvidia shareholders and employees.
Tesla and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the founder and chief executive of the video game publisher Epic Games , were among major industry figures supporting an open letter calling for his return.
But Nvidia sources told CNBC on Monday that the company’s board is not considering bringing him back and is instead focused on a probe into whether his actions harmed American national security.
Pressed repeatedly on whether he accepted the U.S. intelligence on Alice Huang, Trump questioned it.
"I don't know that she's a spy at all. Nobody's proven that," he said. "He probably shouldn't have been doing, on a personal basis, what he did. You know, from — who knows? That's a different story. But nobody's proven that she's a spy. She may not be a spy."
Trump earlier offered a broader version of the same claim. "Usually what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Trump said. "I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
Asked whether he trusted the U.S. intelligence that the woman was a Chinese agent, and whether Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him so, Trump said he had not heard it.
"Who told me that? ... I haven't heard that. I haven't heard that," he said. "No, I don't know that she is a spy."
The president’s claims do not square exactly with what is publicly known about U.S. officials’ concerns over the affair.
According to The New York Times, Rubio was so alarmed by what intelligence officials were learning about Alice Huang through electronic surveillance that he drafted a classified memorandum on her alleged recruitment and briefed Trump on it aboard Air Force One in May, en route to China.
But Trump brushed aside warnings from Rubio and nonetheless pressed ahead with a relationship that saw Huang become a frequent White House visitor after donating $25 million to the president's ballroom project.
The president defended the decision to keep selling chips to China and brushed aside the suggestion that his closeness to Huang had endangered national security. "It was not put at risk," he said Monday, before pivoting to a claim that the country "is now stronger than ever before."
Trump also dismissed statements from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC last week that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick resisted putting Megaspeed - a China-linked company run by Alice Huang and thought to be a pass-through to help Beijing evade export controls - on his department’s “Entity List” of firms not allowed to purchase American products.
Asked about that, Trump said Lutnick "might have delayed it, but he was doing that because ... you could have a blowup with China."
"One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China. Different views," Trump said, declining to say whether he would replace Lutnick, who is traveling with him to China aboard Air Force One despite the scandal surrounding him and is scheduled to testify on the Nvidia affair before Congress in the next few weeks.
Huang was barred from selling Nvidia's most advanced processors, including its Blackwell line, to China, a restriction Trump defended while playing down its stakes.
"The only thing he was able to sell to China were chips that were sort of obsolete, a little bit like our avionics," Trump said. "Selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing."
The president said he might raise the alleged spying operation with Chinese President Xi Jinping when the two leaders meet on Thursday but would not commit to doing so when pressed by reporters.
"I'll ask him what I want to ask him," he said.

articles.title_orig: New Data Paves the Way for Weight-Loss Drugs for Young Children, but Questions Remain
articles.title_zh: New Data Paves the Way for Weight-Loss Drugs for Young Children, but Questions Remain
articles.content_orig:
New results from a closely watched clinical trial showed that weight-loss drugs are effective for children as young as 6, though some doctors say they are concerned about the prospect of prescribing these medications to such young patients.
The study, presented Monday at the medical conference Obesity Week, examined children ages 6 to 11 who were taking semaglutide, the compound in Ozempic and Wegovy. Most children in the trial had severe obesity, meaning they had a body mass index of 35 or higher. After 68 weeks, nearly 40 percent of those who took the drug no longer had obesity, compared with none of the patients on a placebo.
Novo Nordisk, the drug’s maker, said it would ask the Food and Drug Administration to approve the medication for this age group. The drug is already authorized for children 12 and over. Another new study, also presented at the conference, showed that the weight-loss drug tirzepatide was effective in children age 12 and older.
Doctors widely agree that more needs to be done to address obesity, which affects roughly one in five children and adolescents nationwide. But they are divided over whether powerful GLP-1 drugs, which rewire the brain’s relationship to food, are the right approach. Some are concerned about the potential long-term implications of putting children who are still growing on a drug that erases appetite and can lead people to consume very few calories.
In October, the World Health Organization cautioned against using weight-loss drugs in children under 10, citing a lack of evidence on their effects on children’s growth, development and mental health.
“The question is: Is this the right thing to do?” said Dr. Robert Lustig, a professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco. “Not, does it work? Of course it works. But is it the right thing?”

articles.title_orig: China has ‘normalized’ naval presence near Japan since political spat of 2025
articles.title_zh: China has ‘normalized’ naval presence near Japan since political spat of 2025
articles.content_orig:
NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — In early November, Taiwan’s National Security Council secretary-general tracked more than 100 Chinese military-linked vessels near his island.
But given its scale, the massive flotilla that included coast guard vessels alongside navy warships may have had Taiwan’s maritime neighbor Japan in its sights, military experts say.
They say China has sent an outsized number of its far-seas naval deployments to near Japan’s southernmost islands and nearby waters since a political dispute that erupted in November 2025 over a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Takaichi told a Japanese House of Representatives committee session that month that a Chinese naval blockade or armed conflict involving Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for her own country not far away. China claims self-ruled Taiwan as its own and has not ruled out the use of force to take it.
“There is a direct link between Takaichi’s statement and the quality and quantity of deployments,” said Stephen Nagy, a visiting fellow with the Japan Institute for International Affairs think tank in Tokyo. “(China) is also sending a signal to Tokyo that if it continues its current position vis-a-vis Taiwan that Beijing will continue these activities.”
China is using the deployments, including live-fire drills, uncrewed drone missions and voyages by entire aircraft carrier groups, to exert an unrelenting, long-term pressure on Japan without violating international maritime laws, analysts said.
“By repeatedly transiting waters around the (southwestern) Islands, China is gradually normalizing PLA Navy activity within the first island chain, expanding its operational experience and creating a pattern of accepted presence,” said Katsuya Yamamoto, director of the Tokyo-based Sasakawa Peace Foundation’s strategy and deterrence program.
The first island chain includes Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines.
“In other words, it is establishing facts on the ground, or rather at sea, that broaden its future freedom of action,” Yamamoto said.
In the seven weeks after Takaichi’s comment, the U.S. think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies logged a spike in “notable” PLA escalatory moves. Over 2025 overall, it said, China showed just a “slight increase” in the number of PLA naval vessels reported operating in waters around Japan, including an increase in the number of Chinese ships within the contiguous zone of the disputed Senkaku Islands, which China calls the Diaoyu.
Deployments near the uninhabited, Japanese-controlled Senkakus have “remained at very high levels” over the past year as before, while joint Sino-Russian missions around Japan and Chinese naval activity near the outlying Japanese islets around the Miyako Island “seem to have increased”, said Jeffrey Kingston, a professor specializing in Asian studies and history at Temple University, Japan Campus.
Chinese and Russian aircraft patrolled in June over the Sea of Japan, followed by a joint naval passage in July in the Miyako Strait near outlying Japanese islets. Chinese and Russian surveillance aircraft did five separate flights near Japan in October.
Spokespeople for the Chinese ministries of foreign affairs and national defense have called China’s military actions fair, valid and peaceful.
China is probably using military moves as one in a series of measures – some economic – to get back at Takaichi for her November 2025 remarks, Kingston said. “They haven’t forgotten, that’s for sure,” he said. “They are in various ways trying to put the screws on her.”
Officials in Beijing still want a retraction of the prime minister’s November 2025 comments but it’s unlikely, Kingston believes.
The Japanese government has verbally protested against Chinese military moves, tracked Chinese ships with its own, and scrambled fighter jets.
Tokyo is now considering a 70 trillion to 80 trillion yen (as high as $508 billion) defense spending plan for the five-year period beginning in April 2027, up from 43 trillion yen in the previous half-decade span, Japanese media outlets have reported.
“As the security environment becomes increasingly severe, cooperation with the ally and like-minded countries is indispensable to peace and stability in the region,” Japan’s Ministry of Defense said in an Oct. 29 statement after a meeting with defense officials from Australia, the Philippines and the United States.
The ministry, it said, “will continue to take advantage of various opportunities to further strengthen such cooperation.”

articles.title_orig: Permitting Bill Would Charge Data Centers Billions for Power
articles.title_zh: Permitting Bill Would Charge Data Centers Billions for Power
articles.content_orig:
Weeks after voters lashed out at data centers in the midterms, Congress is debating a sweeping overhaul of federal permitting rules that could help tech companies more quickly build the facilities.
The bill would speed up federal environmental reviews of a variety of energy projects, including transmission lines and gas pipelines, making it easier for developers to get the power they need to run data centers.
But that help comes with a huge catch: Data centers would also have to pay much more for their electricity under a provision in the bill that would charge the facilities extra for access to the electric grid. That measure would upend decades of federal power rules and potentially save billions of dollars over the next decade for households and other ratepayers.
The push to impose higher costs on data centers underscores how thorny the politics around A.I. have become in Washington. Massive, energy-hungry data centers are spreading rapidly across the country, straining electrical networks and triggering anger in many communities . Voters this month approved at least 40 local ballot initiatives to restrict the facilities.
Some environmentalists who oppose the permitting bill have cast it as a boon to tech companies, arguing that the legislation could accelerate the development of data centers powered by natural gas. The bill would pare back federal environmental laws to speed construction of many types of projects, including gas pipelines, wind and solar projects, high-voltage transmission lines, roads, public transit and housing.

articles.title_orig: To Stop Iran’s Rearmament, Trump Must Confront Russia and China
articles.title_zh: To Stop Iran’s Rearmament, Trump Must Confront Russia and China
articles.content_orig:
Click here to download the JINSA Insight
At the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 18–19, President Donald Trump expects to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the summit’s sidelines to discuss getting their assistance in ending the war in Iran, while their two countries are helping sustain Tehran’s war effort. Yet, while the Trump administration has intensified military and economic pressure on Iran, it has simultaneously granted sanctions relief to Russia and refrained from targeting major Chinese financial institutions facilitating Iran’s illicit oil trade.
This contradictory approach risks leaving intact the foreign networks that could finance and rebuild Iran’s postwar rearmament in the event of an accord, as Chinese supplies helped Iran rebuild after the June 2025 12-Day War. Washington must confront the countries enabling Iran’s military recovery, and Shenzhen offers the perfect setting to do so.
Pressure on Iran, Relief for Its Backers
Since the United States and Israel launched Operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion against Iran on February 28, the Trump administration has executed successive campaigns against Tehran’s revenue streams, procurement networks, and smuggling routes. The U.S. naval blockade, first implemented on April 13 and reimposed on July 14, has prevented, according to U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), Iran from earning more than $25 billion in crude oil revenue. The Treasury Department’s Operation Economic Fury , launched in April, targeted the financing infrastructure providing the basis for Iran’s trade and shadow-banking networks. In August, Operation Economic Outcast , or Economic “D-Day,” extended pressure on Tehran’s foreign financial enablers through sanctions and warning of secondary sanctions measures. The most recent initiative, CENTCOM’s Task Force Iron Gate , coordinates efforts against illicit shipments and revenue flows across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea, routes the regime has increasingly utilized because of the U.S. blockade.
Despite these initiatives to go after Iran, Washington has pursued competing policies toward the Islamic Republic’s two primary foreign backers. The administration first provided sanctions waivers on Russian seaborne oil in March, a waiver which it extended twice, allowing Moscow to continue earning revenue from sanctioned oil shipments until the relief ultimately expired in June. In October, the administration authorized temporary transactions for Russian diesel until April 2027 and waived multiple provisions included in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The White House justified the Graham Act waivers by saying enforcing the sanctions provisions “would impede ongoing US efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia.”
Washington has equally shied away from imposing its most consequential financial penalties on China. While the Treasury has imposed sanctions on China’s independent “teapot” oil refineries, Hong Kong-based intermediaries , and procurement companies enabling Iranian trade, it has stopped short of targeting the broader Chinese financial networks that facilitate Iranian oil payments and move the proceeds into the international financial system. When Xi visited Trump in September at the White House, the two extended their trade truce but reached no agreement on Chinese support for Tehran. The administration appears, therefore, reluctant to make any move jeopardizing U.S.-China economic relations even as it attempts to sever Iran’s foreign financial lifelines.
Russia’s Role in Arming Iran
Russia serves as one of Iran’s most consequential military and intelligence suppliers, helping Tehran lead operations against U.S. forces and regional partners. Since March, Moscow has, according to open-source reporting, provided upgraded Geran-2 attack drones , explosives , satellite imagery , and targeting intelligence that bolstered Iranian capabilities during the war. Reports also indicate that Russia is assisting Iran in developing advanced cruise missiles , which would strengthen Tehran’s ability to penetrate regional air defenses. Russia is equally aiding Iran’s strategy of using its proxy network to open a two-front war, as Moscow is reportedly sharing intelligence with the Houthis to carry out attacks on Red Sea shipping.
Russia’s assistance could become even more consequential after a cessation of hostilities. According to The Telegraph , Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, delivered a November 5 letter from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei requesting Russian S-400 air defense systems. Tehran has also pursued Russia’s 4.5-generation Su-35 fighters and will reportedly receive them following the war’s conclusion . A prewar Iranian parliamentary memorandum also obtained by The Telegraph outlined plans to deepen cooperation with Moscow on missiles, drones, and air defenses, suggesting that Tehran views foreign military assistance, especially that from Russia, as a central pillar of its long-term survival. Of course, Russia’s war in Ukraine limits what weaponry it can spare to its Iranian partner, but even selective transfers of air defense components and drone technology would raise the cost of future U.S. or Israeli strikes on Iran’s nuclear and missile facilities.
China’s Role in Financing Iran’s Recovery
China has been more cautious than Russia about transferring complete weapons systems during the ongoing war, but it has played perhaps the largest role in financing Iran’s reconstruction through oil purchases and providing critical components for weapons systems to operate. According to prewar statistics, Beijing bought about 90 percent of Iran’s crude oil exports through independent teapot refineries, making it responsible for an estimated 45 percent of Iran’s total government budget. Iran’s reliance on China has continued during the war, with Kpler data identifying Beijing as the only purchaser of Iranian crude in October. On the weapons front, Chinese firms have supplied Iran with the crucial missile propellant precursor sodium perchlorate , as well as dual-use drone components . The full extent of direct Chinese military assistance during the current war remains uncertain, but the presence of these procurement networks could again accelerate Tehran’s rearmament should hostilities end.
Iran is reportedly constructing more durable infrastructure in China aimed at circumventing U.S. sanctions. According to a recent Iran International report , citing a leaked letter from Iran’s Oil Ministry, Iran now controls a terminal in the Ningbo-Zhoushan free trade zone, holds stakes in docks in Shandong province, and owns seven storage tanks in Dalian, Huizhou, Dongying, Weifang, and Zhoushan. This infrastructure allows tankers in the fleet of Hossein Shamkhani, son of the late Khamenei adviser Ali Shamkhani, 51 of whose vessels the Treasury has sanctioned, to unload near refinery pipelines and allows Iran to store its crude in China before securing buyers, which mitigates the impact of existing Treasury designations and suggests that Iran is building sanctions-resistant oil facilities in China with Beijing’s tacit approval or acquiescence.
The Precedent of the 12-Day War
Iran’s recovery in the wake of previous U.S. and Israeli air campaigns against it is a case in point as to why battlefield success alone cannot guarantee lasting strategic gains. Israel’s October 2024 strikes on Iran reportedly decreased Tehran’s capacity to produce solid fuel for ballistic missiles by approximately 93 percent, from enough for 14 missiles per week to just one. Eight months later, operations during the 12-Day War destroyed additional missile production facilities, launchers, and stockpiles, again reducing Iran’s operational arsenal. articles.title_orig: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’
articles.title_zh: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’
articles.content_orig:
[The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.
Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road."
"I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.
In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.
Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.
In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.
At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint."
"After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."
The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.
Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.
Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.
The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

articles.title_orig: Gemini rolling out 66 new regional voices on Android and iOS, including 10+ UK dialects
articles.title_zh: Gemini rolling out 66 new regional voices on Android and iOS, including 10+ UK dialects
articles.content_orig:
Following a preview at Google I/O , Google is rolling out 66 new regional voices to the Gemini app on both Android and iOS today. The expansion introduces tailored voice options across U.S. English, U.K. English, Indian English, Hindi, Brazilian Portuguese, Indonesian, and Korean.
For users in the UK, the update brings over 10 distinct English voice options covering a wide range of regional cadences. The lineup includes Geordie, Scouse, Brummie, Scottish, Welsh, Northern Irish, Modern RP, and Multicultural London English (MLE).
This might help reduce the issues that sometimes still occur when English accents , in particular, morph into a hybrid of Australian or even American that has been going on for a while with Gemini Live. We have not yet been able to test to confirm this has been resolved with the update. As someone with a regional English accent, this extra representation with Gemini voices is quite welcome.
According to Google, these voices are tuned for natural pronunciation, pitch, and everyday local rhythm rather than exaggerated stereotypes. Because the focus is on cadence over slang, Gemini will sound like a local without filling its text responses with forced street slang. Once selected, your chosen voice carries across the entire app, applying to both Gemini Live conversations and standard text-to-speech playback when tapping the “Listen” icon on chat responses.
You can preview and select the new options today by tapping the three-dot menu inside Gemini Live, or by heading into the Gemini app settings and selecting “Gemini’s voice.” It’s worth noting that the voices aren’t explicitly labeled by city or region in the app menu, and Gemini isn’t programmed to self-identify which accent it is using if you ask it directly.
Instead, Google notes that locally rooted prompts about food, culture, or sport, such as asking for the best pub in Sheffield for a Sunday roast – my suggestion is not a pub; it’s Turnip & Thyme on Eccleshall Road, FWIW. Or another suggestion from big G is where to find proper ingredients for a traditional Scouse stew; the company says these will naturally bring out the warmth and rhythm of the new dialects.
I’d suggest trying to ask where to get the best pattie and chips in Hull or where to get the best pint in Leeds (it’s Whitelocks).

articles.title_orig: The Nvidia scandal fuels tougher China chip rules as Commerce targets Singapore and Malaysia
articles.title_zh: The Nvidia scandal fuels tougher China chip rules as Commerce targets Singapore and Malaysia
articles.content_orig:
The Commerce Department announced Monday it is cracking down on a loophole that has allowed Chinese firms to skirt export controls on American AI chips.
It marks the first government response since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from his multitrillion-dollar chipmaker after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy — and as romances with at least two Nvidia employees surfaced.
The department’s Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule that seeks to close a loophole that Chinese firms have used to lease Nvidia’s advanced computing power by going through data centers in third countries, according to a Monday press release .
It was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council,” according to the release.
It came after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized the Commerce Department for not acting sooner against Megaspeed — an Nvidia customer for whom Huang lover Alice Huang, no relation, worked –which has been accused of illegally diverting sensitive AI chips to China.
A license will now “be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion,” according to the new rule .
Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned President Trump about the former Nvidia boss’ romance with Alice Huang last spring, according to reports. Last week, Jensen Huang resigned following bombshell revelations about that relationship and an affair with senior Nvidia exec Kimberly Powell.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s team for the Chinese spy mess, saying the Treasury, State Department, Defense Department and US Trade Representative had been trying “for months” to blacklist Megaspeed.
In a Sunday letter addressed to Lutnick, Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington – the top Dem on the Senate commerce committee – urged the commerce secretary to reinforce export controls on the sale of AI chips to China.
Chinese firms like Alibaba and ByteDance have “used overseas data centers equipped with advanced Nvidia chips to train advanced AI models,” she wrote. “These companies are exploiting a loophole in US export controls by using advanced American chips in foreign data centers even when those chips are restricted from the [People’s Republic of China].
“Despite warnings from the Bureau of Industry and Security that certain arrangements may violate existing restrictions, the Department of Commerce failed to close this loophole, allowing PRC companies to advance their AI capabilities using sensitive American technology.”
Asked about reports that Rubio had briefed Trump on the alleged Chinese spy plot targeting Huang, the president said Monday, “I haven’t heard that.”
“I don’t know that she [Alice Huang] is a spy,” the commander-in-chief told reporters as he left the White House for a trip to the Philippines and China. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy.”
Trump also said that the national security of the country “was not put at risk” and that he “would not mind” if Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO.
Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named as interim CEO , and the chipmaking giant has hired an outside firm to seek a permanent replacement.
With Huang, one of the driving forces of the AI boom, missing in action, investors have been panicking that Nvidia’s dealmaking could slow — a potentially massive monkey wrench for the sector after recent weeks have seen Wall Street get jittery about the tech trade.

articles.title_orig: Cantwell calls out U.S. Secretary of Commerce for allowing China access to advanced AI technology
articles.title_zh: Cantwell calls out U.S. Secretary of Commerce for allowing China access to advanced AI technology
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.content_orig:
President backs Lutnick after treasury secretary Scott Bessent blamed commerce department for delays in blocking advance AI chip exports
Sign up for the Breaking News US email
Donald Trump also defended his commerce secretary Howard Lutnick today, after he came under fire for allegedly slow-walking export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China. This comes after the company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, was ousted from his role following a revelation that he had a close relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), allegedly a Chinese operative.
Lutnick is now set to testify before Congress about delays by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration.
Today, Trump justified any delayed action by Lutnick, adding that he’s done a “very good” job. “If you didn’t delay it, if you did do something, you could have a blow up with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said.
Lutnick is currently traveling with the president and other senior officials and cabinet members to Manila.
Meanwhile, Scott Bessent , Trump’s treasury secretary, said in an intervie with CNBC that he has “for months” been in favor of putting Megaspeed on the blacklist – but Lutnick’s commerce department “has the pen”.
“You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he added on Friday.
Today, Trump said he understood both officials’ perspectives.
“One wants to be friendly with China and one wants to have a blowup with China. They both are acceptable but they are different views,” the president told reporters.
A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, according to officials. The USS Theodore Roosevelt has now been deployed to the “area of responsibility”, US Central Command (Centcom) said on Monday. The carrier joins the USS George HW Bush and USS George Washington.
Centcom said that move is “part of a scheduled deployment”, even though the US war with Iran enters its ninth month and peace talks have stalled.
Until April this year, the presence of three warships in the region hadn’t been seen since 2003 during the Iraq war.
Last week, Trump has said that the war in Iran is “effectively over” as he played down concerns that the US would escalate its military campaign against Tehran after the midterm elections.
“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters during a briefing at the White House.

Today, Trump justified any delayed action by Lutnick, adding that he’s done a “very good” job. “If you didn’t delay it, if you did do something, you could have a blow up with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said. This comes after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC last week that he has been pushing “for months” to add Megaspeed, the data center company led by an alleged Chinese spy who was reportedly in a relationship with ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, to the US trade blacklist. But, Bessent added, Lutnick’s Commerce Department “has the pen” on the decision. Today, Trump said he understood both officials’ perspectives. “One wants to be friendly with China and one wants to have a blowup with China. They both are acceptable but they are different views,” the president told reporters.
Democrat Mary Peltola is leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the nail-biting race for US Senate in Alaska. With 97% of the ballots counted, Peltola – a former congresswoman – has 49.9% of the vote and only needs more than 50% to win. At present, Sullivan only has 46% of the vote. This would be the Democrats’ ninth flip of the midterms cycle and the first time the party has won a US Senate since 2009.
⁠Trump also said today that he ⁠would ​“not ‌mind” ‌seeing Jensen ‌Huang reinstated as the chief executive ‌officer of ​Nvidia. The president added that the suggestion that Huang could return to Nvidia is not a bad idea. He says the ex-CEO has learned a lesson, and denied that national security has been put at risk.
The president also continued to shift responsibility to Joe Biden administration for the nationwide ground stop over the weekend, that saw thousands of flights. Trump also said that he needed more funding to overhaul the outdated telecommunication system responsible for the disruptions. This, despite Congress passing a $12.5bn air traffic control package in 2025. More here
The Trump administration has warned Elizabeth Warren , the senior Democratic senator expected to chair the powerful Senate banking committee, she could face “significant legal consequences” if she fails to preserve records related to investigations into Donald Trump . US attorney Aaron Reitz of the southern district of Texas sent Warren a warning letter, stating that she appears “eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates”. The letter mirrors other warnings that Department of Justice officials have sent to Democratic lawmakers who have indicated they will investigate the Trump administration when the party becomes the majority in Congress next year.
Democrats may have secured the Senate majority, but one key contest is still ahead. Over the coming weeks, Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen , along with any late challengers, will vie for the party’s top Senate leadership post before lawmakers cast their votes. Here are four things to know about how the election works.
A secret, closed-door election: Unlike the public Speaker of the House vote, where lawmakers cast ballots on the chamber floor, the Senate leadership contest takes place behind closed doors. Senators vote by secret ballot, and individual votes are not disclosed.
The winner only needs a caucus majority: The Democratic leadership race is decided solely by members of the party’s Senate caucus. If Democrats hold 55 seats, a candidate would need 28 votes to win. If Democrat Mary Peltola wins in Alaska and the party reaches 56 seats, the threshold rises to 29 votes.
The vote is scheduled for next month: As things stand, the election is set for 1 December . Both incumbent senators and incoming Democratic members will participate, while retiring and outgoing senators will not vote, despite many having publicly weighed in on the race.
Republicans choose their leaders separately: Republicans hold their own closed-door leadership elections in both chambers. Earlier this month, House Republicans selected hardliner Jim Jordan as their leader after Mike Johnson opted not to run for minority leader. In the Senate, Republicans unanimously backed John Thune to continue leading the conference.
As the leadership battle for Senate majority leader heats up between progressive Democrat Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer , the current minority leader, we’re watching for more on how the two are securing support of the wider caucus.
While several Democrats have said they don’t intend to back Schumer, they haven’t necessarily pledged to support Van Hollen.
Democratic Senator-elect Josh Turek , who flipped Iowa’s open seat in the recent midterms, told reporters today that he’d spoken to both lawmakers but is still waiting for “further plans” from them about how they will deal with affordability in the US.
“I like both,” Turek added. “I have not given my allegiance to any leadership or any party, and I told Iowans I was going to sit down with them and say: ‘What are you going to do for Iowa?’”

The rapid proliferation of hyperscale data centres (HDCs) in the USA—mainly driven by the adoption of artificial intelligence—has raised concerns about this industry’s carbon footprint. We compiled facility-level information on 403 US hyperscale data centres operating between May 2024 and April 2025 and estimated their electricity consumption, electricity sources and attributable CO 2 emissions. Across facility-load scenarios, these HDCs consumed approximately 68–99 TWh of electricity and were associated with approximately 21–31 million metric tons of CO 2 under a location-based, total-output balancing-authority attribution method. Under the central scenario, HDC electricity demand was approximately 82 TWh, corresponding to about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption, and attributable CO 2 emissions were approximately 25.7 Mt. Roughly 54% of attributed generation was supplied by fossil-fuel sources. The HDC electricity-weighted total-output carbon intensity was approximately 314 gCO 2 kWh −1 , compared with a US total-output average of approximately 348 gCO 2 kWh −1 . Our approach provides a facility-resolved attributional framework for assessing the carbon footprint of hyperscale data centres using plant-level electricity-generation and emissions data.

Access to the restricted facility-level dataset may be considered for approved research collaborations, subject to the underlying data-use agreement, provider authorization and execution of an appropriate data-use agreement. Requests may be directed to the corresponding author. We provide public state- and balancing-authority-level data exports containing the electricity demand, attributable CO 2 emissions, total-output carbon intensity and attributed fuel mix used in the revised analysis. These aggregate exports reflect the central facility-load scenario ( u = 0.58) and the total-output attribution basis used for the headline results. They are available through the public reproducibility repository 46 . The repository exports, rather than the separate visualization interface, constitute the authoritative public data products for the revised analysis. Because the underlying facility data are protected by a data-use agreement, raw facility identifiers, addresses, coordinates and commercially sensitive facility attributes are not publicly released. The complete facility-level map-generation workflow requires authorized access to those inputs. Access to facility-level map coordinates remains subject to provider authorization and the data-use agreement; public aggregate files do not substitute for the restricted facility-level observations. Source data are provided with this paper.
All code used to estimate HDC power capacity, evaluate the capacity model, compute electricity use and emissions, validate public aggregate exports and reproduce manuscript-facing numerical results is publicly available in the public reproducibility repository 46 . A tagged snapshot corresponding to the Round 3 reproducibility materials is available as version v0.3.1-round3-final 47 . The repository contains: (1) the fully specified scikit-learn capacity-model pipeline, including disclosed predictors, preprocessing, effective hyperparameters, software version and evaluation metrics; (2) a non-identifying 403-row synthetic facility fixture with six missing power-capacity values; (3) a deterministic public synthetic split artefact at results/tables/synthetic_validation/splits.json , together with random and grouped validation outputs; (4) REPRO.md , documenting the validation sample, explicit imputation indicator, software versions, restricted-data workflow and emissions-accounting conventions; (5) scripts/reproduce_model.py , which regenerates the public synthetic validation outputs and writes the deterministic split artefact; (vi) the total-output emissions-attribution workflow using EPA eGRID2023 Revision 2; (7) denominator-audit, plant-inventory, public-export, restricted-data and manuscript-output validation scripts and (8) aggregate state- and balancing-authority-level exports used to verify the headline results. The public synthetic and aggregate materials allow external researchers to execute the capacity-model validation workflow, verify the emissions denominator, reproduce headline scenario totals, sum the public regional exports and run the repository tests without access to restricted facility records.
